microtopics.badge_reason: Learner must explain why a digit rotation's invariant depends on original length, then diagnose the distinct two-digit-prefix exception.
entry_assumptions: Decimal place value and powers of ten.

microtopics.inferential_jump: Explain why changing original length changes a place-value sign and flips whether a rotation preserves divisibility; under two-digit rotation the odd-length exception is different.

teaching_path.action: Use the decimal identity 10 congruent to -1 modulo 11: each shift by one decimal place changes the residue sign.
teaching_path.output: Sign-change mechanism independent of a particular digit string.

teaching_path.action: Compare two-digit 10u+v with digit-swapped 10v+u as a neutral worked anchor.
teaching_path.why_valid: Modulo11, the respective remainders are v-u and u-v.
teaching_path.output: For two positions, swapping negates residue, including zero.

teaching_path.action: Represent a general L-digit input with leading digit a and remaining value B as N=a×10^(L−1)+B; its one-digit left rotation is R=10B+a.
teaching_path.why_valid: Shifting the suffix left multiplies by ten and appending a adds its units value.
teaching_path.output: Exact positional equations, not the final parity classification.

teaching_path.action: Identify the assumption that must be rechecked whenever a two-digit demonstration is generalized to another original length.
teaching_path.why_valid: The contribution of a is multiplied by ten L−1 times; changing L changes that exponent.
teaching_path.output: Audit length and leading zero conventions before deciding the invariant.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Rotating a multiple of11 preserves divisibility for every digit length because it works for 22 and 1210.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Why does 121 rotate to 211, but 1210 rotates to 2101? Are these outcomes explained by the unchanged digit sum?
misconceptions.repair: Use the positions of digits modulo11. N=a10^(L−1)+B and R=10B+a; exponent parity, not digit sum, controls sign changes.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: If rotation creates an initial zero, the original digit length changes and so should the rule.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Does 110 rotating two digits to 011 make the original three-digit statement into a two-digit one?
misconceptions.repair: Keep the original fixed-width L positions throughout each rotation; a new leading zero changes value but not the definition of the input operation.

exit_task.prompt: For any three-digit integer 100a+10b+c (a from1..9, b,c from0..9), explain why 11 divides it exactly when the alternating digit sum a-b+c is 0 OR 11, not just 0. Check 209.

answer.summary: The alternating sum can equal 0 or11.
reasoning: The allowed digit bounds make −8≤a−b+c≤18. The only multiples of11 in this interval are 0 and 11.
answer.check: 121 has sum0; 209 has sum11; both are divisible by11.

accepted: For original N=a10^(L−1)+B with a nonzero first digit and rotation R=10B+a, modulo11 N≡a(-1)^(L−1)+B and R≡a−B. If L is even, R≡−N, so zero stays zero. If L is odd and N≡0, B≡−a, so R≡2a, nonzero because a is 1..9.
rejected: Digit sum stays constant so mod11 divisibility always stays constant.
The odd-length counterexample 121 is an arithmetic accident.

questions.stem: For decimal digits u and v, compare the modulo11 residues of 10u+v and 10v+u. Explain why exchanging their two places negates the residue, without generalizing to every digit length.
conditions: u,v are digits 0..9; this identity is valid even when a digit is zero.

answer.summary: Swapping two places negates modulo11 residue.
reasoning: After swapping, 10v+u≡u−v, exactly the negative residue.
If the original residue is zero, its negative is zero, but this two-place anchor says nothing yet about all digit lengths.
answer.check: Compare 37 versus73 (opposite nonzero residues) and22 versus22 (zero residue).

questions.stem: An L-digit positive integer N is divisible by 11. Move its nonzero FIRST digit to the right end, retaining all original L digit positions, including any new leading zero. Explain WHY divisibility by 11 is preserved whenever L is even but cannot be preserved when L is odd. Make the causal contrast between 1210 → 2101 and 121 → 211; giving only numerical checks is not an explanation.
conditions: Original L≥2 and positive L-digit N is divisible by11.
B represents the suffix of length L−1, with zeros permitted.
After rotation, a new leading zero is retained as a position.

answer.summary: For an initial multiple of11, one-leading-digit left rotation preserves divisibility exactly at even original length.
reasoning: Let original N=a10^(L−1)+B, with a in1..9 and suffix B of fixed length L−1. Rotated R=10B+a.
If original L is even then N≡B−a and R≡a−B≡−N, so an initial zero remainder remains zero.
If L is odd and 11|N then 0≡N≡a+B, hence B≡−a and R≡2a, nonzero modulo11 because 1≤a≤9.
For four-digit 1210, rotation 2101 is divisible by11. For three-digit 121, rotation 211 is not.

reasoning_route.action: Maintain original L and leading digit a, with suffix B and zero-safe rotation.
reasoning_route.why_valid: The defined operation has a fixed original number of positions.
reasoning_route.output: N and R retain comparable positions.

reasoning_route.action: Express N=a10^(L−1)+B and R=10B+a and reduce modulo11.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Rotation shifts all suffix positions and appends a units digit; 10≡−1 modulo11.

reasoning_route.action: Explain why the exponent's parity makes R either −N or the nonzero 2a residue when 11|N.
reasoning_route.why_valid: For even L the sign on a is negative; for odd L it is positive, and a is 1..9 so 11∤2a.
reasoning_route.output: Even original L preserves; odd L cannot.

reasoning_route.action: Compare 1210→2101 and 121→211 as independent changed-length checks.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Both inputs are divisible by11 but have different original length parity.
reasoning_route.output: Observed results agree with causal rule.

answer.check: 1210→2101: 11 divides both; 121→211: only 121 is divisible by11; independently try 110→101 and 1232→2321.

questions.stem: The operation CHANGES: instead of moving ONE leading digit, move the first TWO digits as one block to the right end (original L≥3). An original L-digit integer N is divisible by11. Explain why the new rotation always preserves 11-divisibility at even L, while for odd L it survives exactly when the original two-digit prefix A is itself divisible by11. Account for the contrasting odd-length cases 110 → 011 and 121 → 112.
conditions: L≥3 and the original L-digit positive integer is divisible by11.
Two-digit prefix A is between10 and99 and suffix C uses exactly L−2 digits, with zero padding allowed.
Rotate the first TWO digits as a block; retain the original width L.
Leading zeros produced by rotation do not change original L.

answer.summary: Two-leading-digit rotation preserves 11-divisibility for even L, or for odd L exactly when the original prefix A is divisible by11.
reasoning: Write N=A10^(L−2)+C and R=100C+A for two-digit prefix A=10a+b and padded suffix C.
Modulo11, 100≡1 and R≡C+A. If L even, L−2 even, so N≡A+C and the rotated residue equals the original residue, preserving zero.
If L odd, N≡−A+C=0 gives C≡A; R≡2A. Because 2 and11 are coprime, this is zero iff A is divisible by11.
For odd length, 110 (A=11) rotates as 011=11 and succeeds; 121 (A=12) rotates to112 and fails.

reasoning_route.action: Group first two digits as A and keep the original L−2 suffix C.
Explain the even-length equality of residues and odd-length residue2A when N is divisible by11.
reasoning_route.why_valid: 100≡1 modulo11; sign of 10^(L−2) depends on parity of L.
reasoning_route.output: Even L always works; odd L depends on A.
The original prefix A can equal 11,22,...,99.

reasoning_route.why_valid: Both have odd original length but only the first prefix is multiple11.

answer.check: 110→011 (11, divisible by11); 121→112 (not divisible); 11220→22011 (both divisible with A=11).
